title: Citing Sources Correctly From the Very First Draft
summary: Learn how to cite sources correctly from your first IB Extended Essay draft, manage evidence, avoid plagiarism, and prepare for fall feedback.
body_markdown:
Citing sources correctly from the very first draft is one of the safest habits an IB student can develop. For students drafting an **IB Extended Essay during the September-November fall term** , it prevents lost page numbers, unclear paraphrasing, incomplete references, and stressful corrections before supervisor meetings.


The central rule is simple: whenever you use another person's words, ideas, data, images, methods, or other intellectual work, acknowledge the source **at the point where you use it** . A bibliography entry alone is not enough. Readers must be able to identify borrowed material and locate its source.


### What the IB officially expects


The IB's[Effective citing and referencing guide](https://www.ibo.org/contentassets/76d2b6d4731f44ff800d0d06d371a892/effective-citing-and-referencing-en.pdf) distinguishes between two connected processes:


- **Citing** identifies a source in the body of your work at the point of use.
- **Referencing** provides the fuller publication details needed to locate that source.


The IB requires acknowledgment of sources, but it does **not prescribe one universal citation style** for every candidate. Your school, department, or supervisor may require APA, MLA, Chicago, Harvard, or another recognized system. Follow that local instruction consistently.


The[IB academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) explains that copied, adapted, paraphrased, and translated material must be acknowledged. This principle applies to books, articles, data, maps, diagrams, photographs, interviews, code, datasets, and AI-generated material.


The[official IB Extended Essay overview](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/extended-essay/) describes the EE as independent research culminating in a **4,000-word paper** . Independence means selecting, interpreting, evaluating, and synthesizing evidence while making your own reasoning visible. It does not mean working without sources.


### Why citations belong in the first draft


Students sometimes write an uncited draft and plan to insert references later. After several weeks, however, it becomes difficult to remember which sentence came from which article, whether wording was copied exactly, or where a statistic appeared.


Retrofitting citations can also obscure how sources contribute to a paragraph. Several authors' ideas may be combined without showing where one contribution ends and another begins. Even if every author appears in the bibliography, individual claims remain difficult to trace.


Citing during drafting helps you:


- Preserve page numbers and precise source details
- Separate your analysis from borrowed ideas
- Identify unsupported claims before feedback
- Show your supervisor how the argument developed
- Turn the final reference check into an audit rather than a reconstruction exercise


RevisionDojo's guide to[best practices for IB EE and IA citations](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/10-best-practices-for-citing-sources-properly-in-ib-ee-and-ia) provides a useful final check, but the system should begin during research.


### Build a source system before writing


Create a source log as soon as you begin reading. A spreadsheet, reference manager, or organized document is sufficient if you use it consistently.


Record the following for each source:


- Author or responsible organization
- Full title and publication date
- Publisher, journal, volume, issue, and DOI where relevant
- Stable URL and access date when required
- Exact page numbers for useful passages
- Whether each note is a quotation, paraphrase, or personal response
- The claim or EE section the source may support


Notes become risky when copied wording and personal commentary look identical. Label material as **QUOTE** , **PARAPHRASE** , or **MY ANALYSIS** , or use a consistent color system.


Citation generators can accelerate formatting, but they cannot detect every missing detail or judge source quality. The[RevisionDojo Citation Tool](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/citation-tool) can help create and save references, but check each entry against your school's required style and the original source.


### Cite quotations, paraphrases, and data correctly


A direct quotation reproduces exact wording. It needs quotation marks or block formatting, a citation or note, and normally a page number when the source provides pages.


A paraphrase expresses a source's idea using genuinely new language and sentence structure. It still requires a citation because changing the wording does not make the idea yours. Replacing a few words with synonyms while retaining the original structure is not an adequate paraphrase.


A practical method is to read the passage, hide it, explain the idea from memory, and then reopen the source to check accuracy. Attach the citation immediately. This helps preserve your own voice without losing attribution.


Statistics, definitions, datasets, theories, historical interpretations, and specialized factual claims also require citations. Common knowledge may not, although this depends on the subject and audience. If a reasonable reader could ask, "How do you know this?", a reliable source is usually appropriate.


Strong citation formatting cannot rescue weak evidence. RevisionDojo's overview of the[best sources for IB Extended Essay research](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-are-the-best-sources-for-ib-extended-essay-research) explains how authority, relevance, and methodology affect source selection.


### Attach evidence to specific claims


A citation placed only at the end of a long paragraph can have an unclear scope. Readers should know whether it supports one sentence, several connected statements, or the whole discussion.


Use a **claim, evidence, analysis** structure:


1. State a limited, defensible claim.
2. Present relevant evidence with an immediate citation.
3. Explain how the evidence supports, qualifies, or challenges the claim.
4. Evaluate limitations or competing interpretations.
5. Connect the reasoning to the research question.


Citation density is not the same as analytical quality. A paragraph containing several quotations but little explanation remains source-driven. Your task is to interpret evidence and justify conclusions. RevisionDojo's guide to[integrity and original argumentation in the EE](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/integrity-in-the-ib-extended-essay-honest-research-and-original-argumentation) explains how transparent sourcing and independent reasoning work together.


### Use a September-November citation routine


### September: establish the system


Confirm the required style with your supervisor, create your source log, and save stable copies of important material. Record complete details before drafting, especially for PDFs, datasets, and sources that may later move behind a login or paywall.


### October: cite while drafting


Insert citations as soon as evidence enters a paragraph. If a detail is temporarily unavailable, use a visible marker such as **\[PAGE NUMBER NEEDED\]** . Resolve it during the same week's research session rather than accumulating placeholders.


### November: conduct a two-way audit


Check every in-text citation against the final list, then check every final-list entry against the essay. This reveals missing references and unused entries. RevisionDojo's explanation of an[EE reference list versus a bibliography](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ee-reference-list-vs-bibliography-difference) clarifies the terminology your school may use.


### Common mistakes to correct early


Avoid these recurring problems:


- Citing quotations but not paraphrased ideas
- Listing a source without citing it in the essay
- Omitting available page numbers from quotations
- Presenting a secondary summary as the original source
- Providing a URL without author, title, or publication details
- Forgetting to source adapted tables, figures, and graphs
- Trusting citation software without checking its output


Always reopen the source and confirm that it supports the precise claim you have written.


### Citing AI-assisted material


IB academic integrity guidance requires AI-generated output used in assessed work to be acknowledged appropriately. Depending on current school policy and citation style, you may need to document the tool, output, prompt, and date.


Do not paste generated paragraphs into an EE and present them as your own. Jojo AI can help you examine argument clarity, source quality, or possible citation gaps, but responsibility for authorship and accuracy remains yours. Keep a record of meaningful assistance and confirm disclosure requirements with your supervisor.


### Conclusion


Citing sources correctly from the first draft makes an IB EE more credible, traceable, and manageable. Use your school's required style, capture complete details during research, cite quotations and paraphrases at the point of use, and audit citations in both directions.
